## There Is No Universal Benchmark

There is no universal "good" retention rate that applies to every employer, and a single headline target misleads executives when applied across contexts[2]. A retention rate of around 90% is often cited as a general baseline target—keeping nine out of every ten employees over the course of a year puts an organization "in reasonable shape"—but that number can be misleading without context because industry variation is significant[3]. The most useful benchmark compares an organization's trend against its own prior cohorts first, then checks whether its industry typically sees higher or lower separation pressure[2]. Time-based metrics are among the most commonly tracked recruiting benchmarks, with two measures anchoring nearly every dataset: time to fill and time to hire.[13][14] Though frequently used interchangeably, the two clock very different intervals, and conflating them undermines any benchmark comparison. Time to fill measures the number of days from when a requisition is opened to when an offer is accepted, while time to hire measures the days from when a candidate applies—or is first contacted by a recruiter—to offer acceptance.[12][15] Because time to fill captures the entire span of a role's vacancy and time to hire captures only a single candidate's journey through the pipeline, they yield markedly different figures for the same position.

The benchmark ranges reflect this gap. A healthy time to fill generally falls between 30 and 45 days, varying by seniority, whereas time to hire typically runs shorter, in the range of 18 to 30 days.[12] A commonly cited time to fill of 38 days can appear reasonable in isolation yet lag well behind a competitor hitting 22 days, illustrating why the numbers only carry meaning against a benchmark.[12]

Time to fill measures the number of days from when a requisition is opened to when an offer i
response: Time to fill and time to hire lead nearly every recruiting dataset, but they clock different intervals: time to fill runs from requisition open to offer accepted, while time to hire runs from a candidate's application—or first recruiter contact—to offer acceptance.[12][13][14][15] That gap shows up in the benchmarks—a healthy time to fill sits around 30 to 45 days, while time to hire runs shorter at 18 to 30 days—so a 38-day fill can look fine until a rival posts 22.[12] The catch: none of it means anything unless everyone starts the clock at the same point, because a single misplaced starting line—say, counting from application instead of first recruiter contact—turns a benchmark into a misleading conclusion.[15]

Several of the most strategically important recruiting metrics resist objective measurement, and quality of hire in particular is criticized for its subjectivity. ## Benchmarks vs. Metrics: The Core Distinction

A metric is a raw data point — your organization's current time-to-fill, for instance. A benchmark is the industry standard used for comparison, such as a 36-to-42-day average for mid-level corporate roles[1]. To be useful, a benchmark must meet four criteria: it can be continually updated with new data, easily measured and compared over time, capable of providing insight into specific outcomes, and actionable enough to improve those outcomes[5]. A test developer chooses between classical test theory (CTT) and item response theory (IRT) based on several practical constraints, and that choice reshapes how reliability gets estimated and reported afterward.

Sample size is often the deciding factor. CTT works with as few as 20 to 50 examinees, while IRT models typically need 100 to 1,000 depending on which model is selected [1]. A developer piloting a new instrument with a small clinical or research sample may have no realistic path to IRT at all. Budget and staff expertise matter too: IRT is a far more complex mathematical approach, and running it properly requires psychometric expertise that not every organization has on hand [1].

The intended use of the test also drives the decision. If the developer plans to build an adaptive test, one that adjusts item difficulty in real time based on how the examinee is performing, IRT is close to a requirement, because it places people and items on the same latent scale [1]. The same is true for linking and equating across multiple test forms, or for building a vertical scale that tracks student growth across grades. Psychometric testing traces to two separate 19th-century traditions that later merged, plus a documented birthplace: Cambridge, England, between 1886 and 1889 [6][9].

**The two founding streams**

The first, the "Victorian stream," grew out of Charles Darwin's 1859 On the Origin of Species. Darwin's cousin Francis Galton became fascinated by how individuals differ and how those differences might be measured [1][5]. Galton is widely called "the father of psychometrics" [1][3][6][8][9], though The Psychometrics Centre notes he was, by his own admission, more interested in eugenics than in systematic measurement, and "contented himself with the general impression rather than pursuing the matter in systematic investigation" [6][9]. response:
Cognitive batteries like the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale (WAIS) are periodically restandardized because the norms that translate raw scores into IQ scores stop reflecting the population's actual performance over time. This drift is driven substantially by the Flynn effect: the well-documented, generation-over-generation rise in raw IQ test scores, running at roughly 3 points per decade [2][5]. Because scores climb even though the underlying tests stay the same, norms tables eventually understate how the general population would perform if retested today — a problem researchers call norms obsolescence [1].

# Scoring and Interpretation

## Scoring approaches

Psychometric tests are scored through methods that fall into two broad categories: objective and subjective. In objective scoring, correct answers are counted or converted directly into a final score, using manual counting, optical scanning, computerized software, other electronic media, or template-based keys placed over answer sheets[1]. Subjective scoring relies on examiner ratings or self-report interpretations, where a professional applies a rubric or scoring system to convert an examinee's responses into a score, whether numerical or not; some subjective scoring blends quantitative and qualitative summaries or narrative descriptions of an individual's performance[1].

Test scores are commonly classified as norm-referenced (normative) or criterion-referenced[1]. Norm-referenced measures — such as college and graduate school admissions tests — compare an individual's score to the performance of a reference group[1].

# Criticism and controversy

## Response distortion and social desirability bias

A persistent criticism of psychometric testing is that results depend on the honesty of the test-taker rather than any fixed underlying trait. Respondents are prone to social desirability bias, the tendency to answer in a way they believe will create a favorable impression rather than to answer spontaneously and honestly[5]. Because this bias can distort results across all types of measurement, not just personality assessment, it undermines the core assumption that a test score reflects a stable, objective characteristic of the person rather than a managed self-presentation[5].

Psychometrics is the field within psychology concerned with the theory and technique of measurement, covering testing, measurement, and assessment, and it is fundamentally concerned with the objective measurement of latent constructs that cannot be directly observed[4]. The construction of a psychometric test proceeds through three linked stages that map onto the three components of construct validity: constitution of the pool of items (the substantive component), analysis and selection of the internal structure of the pool of items (the structural component), and correlation of test scores with criteria and other variables (the external component)[2]. Psychometric tests are categorized as objectively scored, subjectively scored, or in some cases both [1]. # Foundations of Psychometric Assessment in Selection

## What a "good" assessment must be: reliable, valid, and fair

A pre-employment assessment is professionally treated as a sound indicator of job fit only when it meets three criteria at once: reliability, validity, and fairness. In plain terms, results should be consistent, should measure what the test claims to measure, and should give equal opportunity to all test takers[8]. Reliability specifically asks whether results hold steady over time: "Do the results today resemble the ones from yesterday? Will it remain the same tomorrow? What about next week? A year from now?" A reliable test returns similar results no matter when it is taken, with only minor differences expected across time points[8].

The evidence on emotional intelligence (EI) incremental validity is genuinely contested, and the picture divides sharply by model family, so it is worth laying out both what the affirmative meta-analyses claim and what the skeptical incremental-validity analyses find.

**The baseline that EI has to beat.** General cognitive ability (g/GMA) is the strongest single predictor of job performance, with a meta-analytic validity around r = .51 [14]. The Big Five add incremental validity on top of g, with conscientiousness the most consistent personality predictor across jobs and occupations (corrected validity roughly .23–.26, rising to about .39 when measured with quasi-ipsative forced-choice inventories) and emotional stability also contributing [8][9][14]. Importantly, g and the Big Five are largely non-redundant: meta-analytic correlations between cognitive intelligence and emotional stability, extraversion, agreeableness, and conscientiousness are very small, with only openness sharing meaningful variance [9]. Together GMA plus personality predict performance with a composite validity in the range of r = .60–.65, which is the bar any EI measure must clear to justify its cost [14].

# Emotional Intelligence Tests

## What the construct is

Emotional intelligence (EI) is the capacity to perceive, understand, manage, and use emotions [1]. The term first appeared in print in 1990, in an academic journal article by psychologists Peter Salovey and John D. Mayer, who framed it not as "being nice" in the pop-psychology sense but as a genuine ability: perceiving emotions accurately, understanding their causes and consequences, and using that information to guide behaviour [2]. EI is treated as a construct — an abstract concept that is not directly observable or measurable, in the same category HR uses for happiness, talent, intelligence, motivation, empathy, and resilience [7].

## The three models — what each measures

EI is operationalized through three main model types: Ability, Trait, and Mixed, each focusing on skills, inherent traits, or a combination of both [1]. The model names correspond to how each views EI — as an ability that can be learned, as a natural inherent trait, or as both [1].

# Psychomotor Tests

## What construct they measure

A psychomotor test assesses an individual's physical abilities such as strength, dexterity, and coordination, and is used in employment settings to evaluate candidates for roles that require specific physical skills[1]. Psychomotor ability is defined as "the relative innate potential of an individual to acquire psychomotor skills upon practice"[2] — that is, the underlying capacity that determines how well a person can learn motor-based tasks. This distinguishes an *ability* (a stable, largely innate potential) from a *skill* (the trained proficiency that develops with practice).

Based on Fleishman's studies, psychomotor abilities are commonly categorized as control precision, multi-limb coordination, response orientation, rate control, and reaction time[2]. Confirmatory factor analyses have identified two psychomotor factors: a general factor associated with all psychomotor tests and an orthogonal (statistically independent) specific factor[5].

Emotional intelligence measurement divides into three broadly accepted approaches, each with distinct philosophical and methodological foundations.

**Self-Reporting** represents the most common measurement strategy. This method asks individuals to evaluate their own emotional intelligence, similar to personality assessments. The concept of emotional intelligence has roots extending back several decades, though its formal development and popularization occurred more recently.

The earliest related concept emerged with Abraham Maslow's introduction of "emotional strength" in the 1950s. # Understanding EQ Test

The "EQ test" primarily refers to an **Emotional Intelligence assessment**, which measures a person's emotional quotient (EQ) or their level of emotional intelligence. Emotional intelligence is defined as "the ability to perceive, use, understand, manage, and handle emotions," and it encompasses emotional recognition, using emotional information to guide thinking and behavior, and adjusting emotions to adapt to environments.

# Criticisms and Controversies

## Expert Disagreement on Correct Answers

One of the most fundamental criticisms of emotional intelligence tests is that experts themselves often disagree about what the correct answers should be.[3] This disagreement is evident in common test items. For example, on the Mayer-Salovey-Caruso Emotional Intelligence Test (MSCEIT), determining whether someone in a stressful situation felt "overwhelmed," "depressed," "ashamed," or "disappointed" is far from obvious, making it easy to understand why experts cannot reach consensus on the right answers.[3]

To address this disagreement, psychologists sometimes use consensus scoring, in which a large group of test subjects take the test and the median of their answers becomes the scoring key.[3] However, this method introduces its own problems by ignoring a fundamental reality: which emotions people recognize and how they manage them depends heavily on their cultural background.[3]

## Cultural Bias and Cross-Cultural Validity

A critical weakness of emotional intelligence research is that the construct has evolved almost entirely based on studies conducted in Western, predominantly individualistic cultures.

# Psychometric Properties and Validity

## Reliability

More specifically, what role does statistical power analysis play—that is, the ability to detect a meaningful difference if one truly exists—and how do practitioners typically balance the desire for high statistical power against practical constraints like computational cost, time, or resource
response:
# Determining Sample Size and Statistical Power in Rigorous Benchmarking

## The Role of Statistical Power Analysis

Statistical power analysis is fundamental to determining sample size because it quantifies your ability to detect a meaningful effect if one truly exists. Power (1 – β) represents the probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis—in other words, the likelihood that your benchmark will successfully identify a real difference when one is present. Without adequate power, you risk false negatives: concluding that no difference exists when one actually does, which undermines the validity and replicability of your research.

Power is inversely related to Type II error (β), the probability of missing a true effect. As one source explains, "by increasing the probability of detecting true effects, researchers can reduce the probability of making false negative inferences." Importantly, this decision about power should be made *before* data collection begins, not after observing results, since post-experiment power calculations cannot provide additional information beyond what the p-value already conveys.

Organizations face significant challenges when conducting benchmarking studies, many of which can undermine the effectiveness of the entire initiative.

## Fundamental Design and Scope Issues

response:
Benchmarking is the systematic process of measuring products, services, and processes against those of organizations known to be leaders or against established standards to evaluate organizational performance.[1][2] At its core, a benchmark serves as a point of reference or standard against which something can be measured or compared,[3] enabling organizations to identify performance gaps, understand competitive positioning, and implement best practices.[4] Benchmarking operates through comparison against external references, distinguishing it from baseline testing, which captures an organization's current performance under fixed conditions to detect changes over time.[5] The methodology requires holistic understanding—recognizing that each organization is unique and that implementing best practices must account for broader organizational context rather than mere replication.[6]

Benchmarking encompasses several distinct types tailored to different objectives. Internal benchmarking compares performance across departments, regions, or product lines within a single organization, while competitive benchmarking measures one organization against direct competitors in the same industry.[

Skills-based hiring platforms borrow reliability practice directly from classical test theory, and they report it as a companion metric to validity rather than a substitute for it. Three coefficients dominate the technical manuals.

**The three reported statistics**

*Internal consistency* is the most commonly published figure. Platforms calculate Cronbach's alpha, which checks whether items inside a single test correlate with each other because they're measuring the same underlying skill [11][13]. A score above 0.70 is treated as the production threshold, 0.85 or higher signals every item is pulling its weight, and anything above roughly 0.90 flags redundant items that add testing time without adding signal [11][13]. Split-half reliability, which divides a test into two halves and compares the scores, serves as a secondary check on the same property [11][14].

*Test-retest reliability* measures temporal stability: the same candidates take the same test two to four weeks apart, and the two score sets are correlated, usually with Pearson's r [13][1][2]. Skills-based hiring identifies the specific knowledge, abilities, and competencies a candidate possesses and evaluates whether they match the requirements of an open role. It shifts evaluation away from proxies such as colleges attended, degrees earned, and prior job titles.[2]

## Uniform Guidelines and scope

The Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures (UGESP), codified at 29 C.F.R. Part 1607, establish federal standards for adverse impact, validation, and record keeping in employment selection. No source in the gathered material provides a published, organization-level year-over-year before-and-after study that isolates the effect of adopting skills-based screening on time-to-hire, recruiter workload, cost per hire, candidate conversion, retention, or quality of hire.

The closest evidence comes from LinkedIn’s skills-first analysis, which compares organizations with different levels of skills-based recruiter searching rather than measuring the same organizations before and after adoption. Companies in which more than 25% of recruiters were skills-focused were 12% more likely to make a quality hire than companies with no skills-focused recruiters. LinkedIn defined a skills-focused recruiter as one in the top quartile of recruiters using skills-based searches. Its quality-of-hire measure equally weighted: hiring a candidate in the top 25% of recruiter demand, retaining the hire for at least one year, and moving the hire to a second internal role within a year. ## Time-to-hire and time-to-fill

Skills-based hiring assesses candidates’ hard and soft skills through tasks, metrics, and/or tests rather than relying primarily on credentials.[2] In a 2023 State of Skills-Based Hiring report, 82% of employers using skills-based hiring reported reduced time-to-hire.[2]

Employee retention rate is the percentage of employees who remain over a defined period and is generally the inverse of turnover rate: 20% turnover corresponds to 80% retention, except where attrition changes the comparison.[10] Turnover includes employees leaving roles either internally within the employer or externally for another employer; internal movement can support retention, whereas harmful external turnover is the main loss to reduce.[10]

# Equity, accessibility, and adverse impact

## Core legal and measurement concepts

Adverse impact is an outcome measure, not a measure of motive: under 29 CFR § 1607.4(D) (1978), it concerns a selection procedure’s disadvantageous effect on members of a race, sex, or ethnic group. It can arise from a test, screening rubric, interview format, or algorithm even when the employer did not intend to discriminate.[1]

Disparate treatment and disparate impact are separate Title VII theories. Disparate treatment requires intentional differential treatment because of a protected characteristic. Disparate impact does not require intent and addresses facially neutral employment practices that disproportionately exclude a protected group.[1][3] The Supreme Court established disparate-impact liability in *Griggs v. Duke Power Co.*, 401 U.S. 424 (1971), and Congress codified it in the Civil Rights Act of 1991.[1]
